title: Suggestion for a sort function
description:
In javascript, there is a built-in function [Array.prototype.sort()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sort) that works on an array (like an R list) and takes a user-defined binary function to define ordering. 

```js
my_array.sort((a, b) => some_function(a, b))
```

Base R functions `sort` and `order` accept atomic vectors only. To sort lists, the user needs to use a combination of indexing with `[` and `order` on some expression. For example, imagine we wanted to sort a list of vectors by length...

```r
x <- list(letters[1:2], letters[1:4], letters, LETTERS) 
sorted_x <- my_list[order(sapply(my_list, length))]
```

The tidy approach could use `dplyr::arrange` on a tibble to sort the list-column.
```r
sorted_x <- tibble(x = x) |> 
  mutate(length = sapply(x, length)) |> 
  arrange(length) |> 
  pull(x)
```

The proposed purrr function would sort a list based on a user-provided function to determine precedence.
```r
# accept a binary function for complex comparisons
sorted_x <- sort_list(.x = x, .f = \(a,b) length(a) < length(b))

# accept a unary function that evaluates to a `sort`-able atomic vector
sorted_x <- sort_list(x, .f = \(a) length(a))
```

This is a reprex to illustrate a simple implementation and use case.

```r
# very minimal implementation of proposed function using quicksort
sort_list <- function(.x, .f) {
  if (length(.x) <= 1)  return(.x)
  if (length(formals(.f)) == 1)  return(.x[order(sapply(.x, .f))])
  pivot <- .x[[1]]
  items <- .x[-1]
  has_precedence <- vapply(items, \(item) .f(item, pivot), logical(1L))  
  before <- sort_list(items[which(has_precedence)], .f)
  after <- sort_list(items[which(!has_precedence)], .f)
  c(before, list(pivot), after)
}

# eg, say need to sort a list of vectors by length
x <- list(letters, letters[1:2], letters[1:4], LETTERS) 

# use proposed function to sort list
x |> sort_list(\(a, b) length(a) < length(b))
x |> sort_list(\(a) length(a))
```

Thanks for your consideration! I'm a huge fan of purrr and tidyverse.

title: Feature request: `Vectorize()` alternative
description:
I wonder if this might be within scope for purrr – sorry if not.

`base::Vectorize()` has some shortcomings:

1.  Its output functions simplify their own output by default if they are closures.
2.  Functions with no arguments, or with `…` as their only argument, are silently returned unchanged. With closures, perhaps this should be an error since they really don't have any arguments to vectorize over. With primitives, any non-dots arguments don't count even if they behave as such. Therefore, if `FUN` is a primitive with one or more non-dots arguments, it might be preferable to consistently return a vectorized closure that wraps the input. Other primitives should probably be errors. Returning the input function unchanged is a problem especially for those primitives that are not vectorized by themselves:

``` r
vectorized_length <- Vectorize(length)
identical(length, vectorized_length)
#> [1] TRUE
# Here, the user may expect `c(a = 10L, b = 26L, c = 1L)`:
vectorized_length(list(a = 1:10, b = letters, c = TRUE))
#> [1] 3
```

<sup>Created on 2023-05-05 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

3.  (Assuming `FUN` is a closure with at least one non-dots argument:) The body of each output function is identical, and it's quite hard to read. This may be confusing, especially because the input function never visibly appears in the output function. This also means it's not useful to copy and paste the printed output function into one's source code.
4.  The arguments are suboptimally named. `vectorize.args` might be renamed to `over`, as in "function `f()` is vectorized over its argument `x`".

``` r
x <- list("foo", "bar")
```

``` r
x <- list("foo", "bar")
```

title: FR: make `list_modify()` aware of pipe's LHS variables
description:
Hi, 

`list_modify()` is a wonderful tool, but it does not keep a reference to the LHS of the pipe.

Therefore, to use it like `dplyr::mutate()`, you should use the `.` placeholder with `magrittr` pipes.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
lst(x = 1) %>% 
  list_modify(x2 = .$x+1)
#> $x
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $x2
#> [1] 2
```

<sup>Created on 2023-01-31 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


However, this is not compatible with native pipe for R versions <4.2 (which have no placeholder). A purist would even go further and advocate against placeholders per se.
Note that many people are stuck with R v4.1 due to external limitations such as with [rstan](https://blog.mc-stan.org/2022/04/26/stan-r-4-2-on-windows/).

It would be great if you could write it `lst(x = 1) %>% list_modify(x2 = x+1)`, just like you would do with `dplyr::mutate()`.

Do you think that is doable?

title: `map()` and `pmap()` remove class from error
description:
I noticed this when googledrive had a test failure, where the function in question uses a `tryCatch()`:

https://github.com/tidyverse/googledrive/blob/7e8fa7abcb220566d2e1e99621b6e5d41e8f1c5b/R/shortcut.R#L184-L187

This `resolve_one()` function ultimately gets called inside `pmap()` and as of v1.0.0, the error no longer has the expected class.

---

With purrr 0.3.5, the class of an error thrown by `.f` is preserved. Here it's an `oops_error`.

``` r
f <- function(x) {
  if (x) {
    cli::cli_abort("oops", class = "oops_error")
  }
  x
}
f(FALSE)
#> [1] FALSE
f(TRUE)
#> Error in `f()`:
#> ! oops

#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. └─global f(TRUE)
#>  2.   └─cli::cli_abort("oops", class = "oops_error")
#>  3.     └─rlang::abort(...)

packageVersion("purrr")
#> [1] '0.3.5'

purrr::map(c(FALSE, TRUE), f)
#> Error in `.f()`:
#> ! oops

#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. └─purrr::map(c(FALSE, TRUE), f)
#>  2.   └─global .f(.x[[i]], ...)
#>  3.     └─cli::cli_abort("oops", class = "oops_error")
#>  4.       └─rlang::abort(...)
err <- rlang::catch_cnd(purrr::map(c(FALSE, TRUE), f))
err
#> <error/oops_error>
#> Error in `.f()`:
#> ! oops
#> ---
#> Backtrace:
#>  1. rlang::catch_cnd(purrr::map(c(FALSE, TRUE), f))
#>  8. purrr::map(c(FALSE, TRUE), f)
#>  9. global .f(.x[[i]], ...)
class(err)
#> [1] "oops_error"  "rlang_error" "error"       "condition"
```

---

But as of v1.0.0, the error no longer has that condition.

``` r
f <- function(x) {
  if (x) {
    cli::cli_abort("oops", class = "oops_error")
  }
  x
}
f(FALSE)
#> [1] FALSE
f(TRUE)
#> Error in `f()`:
#> ! oops

#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. └─global f(TRUE)

#>  3.     └─rlang::abort(...)

#> [1] '1.0.0'

#>  4.     │ └─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>  5.     └─global .f(.x[[i]], ...)
#>  6.       └─cli::cli_abort("oops", class = "oops_error")
#>  7.         └─rlang::abort(...)
err <- rlang::catch_cnd(purrr::map(c(FALSE, TRUE), f))
err
#> <error/rlang_error>
```

title: Find a solution for the inverted chained error problem
description:
In https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/pull/1430 we had an issue where the chained error of `map()` results in a confusing error message.

It seems like any case where we need to pass `error_call` through to `.f` can result in an "inverted" chained error. Really `fn()` is the one calling `map()` here, but it is reported like `map()` called `fn()`, which is quite confusing.

The current hack is to avoid `map()` altogether and switch back to `lapply()`, but that is obviously not great.

We might need something like `with_no_indexed_errors()` that we can wrap the `map()` with to turn off the error chaining. In the tidyr case I don't think we'd ever want to report the index of the failure, and we wouldn't want `map()` mentioned in the error at all.

``` r
library(purrr)
library(rlang)

fn_one <- function(x, error_call = caller_env()) {
  if (x == 3L) {
    abort("Something is wrong.", call = error_call)
  }
  
  x
}

fn <- function(x) {
  error_call <- current_env()
  map(x, \(.x) fn_one(.x, error_call = error_call))
}

fn(1:5)
#> Error in `map()`:
#> ℹ In index: 3.
#> Caused by error in `fn()`:
#> ! Something is wrong.

#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. └─global fn(1:5)
#>  2.   └─purrr::map(x, function(.x) fn_one(.x, error_call = error_call))
#>  3.     └─purrr:::map_("list", .x, .f, ..., .progress = .progress)
#>  4.       ├─purrr:::with_indexed_errors(...)
#>  5.       │ └─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>  6.       └─.f(.x[[i]], ...)
#>  7.         └─global fn_one(.x, error_call = error_call)
#>  8.           └─rlang::abort("Something is wrong.", call = error_call)
```

With `lapply()`:

``` r
fn2 <- function(x) {
  error_call <- current_env()
  lapply(x, \(.x) fn_one(.x, error_call = error_call))
}

fn2(1:5)
#> Error in `fn2()`:
#> ! Something is wrong.

#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. └─global fn2(1:5)
#>  2.   └─base::lapply(x, function(.x) fn_one(.x, error_call = error_call))
#>  3.     └─FUN(X[[i]], ...)
#>  4.       └─global fn_one(.x, error_call = error_call)
#>  5.         └─rlang::abort("Something is wrong.", call = error_call)
```

title: When() should not be depreciated until R 4.3 or later
description:
Continuing the discussion from: [https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/1001](https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/1001)
from mlane
> Why are rbernoulii and when being depreciated and not moved to separate package? In particular "when()" does not have a replacement prior to 4.2.2 because there are bugs in gsub that were only recently patched in the last few months. Why don't simple make a wrapper to the proper function until the next major release of base R? We have strong concerns about the development of R packages and whether users have a voice or if everything has become developer focused. It does not feel like the depreciation is gradual at all. When myself and my teammates read the new changes, we truly felt that the developer of the packages either doesn't understand or they simple don't care how non-developers use there open source package.

from hadley
> I don't understand the connection between when() and gsub()

Gsub did not properly find an replace for 1Gb+ worth of data. 
 https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=18346

In May 2022 a bug was found with gsub/grepl that while it may seem low level basically prevents the data clean up of certain large human resources databases and IOT databases where certain special fields can exceed about 4000 characters.   This is a problem for data clean up of things like--primary spatial database key (PBkey) in [MapInfoPro](https://www.pitneybowes.com/us) map files, the asset_description in [EJWard](https://www.ejward.com/fuel-management-software/), the customer issue description/resolution in [Salesforce](https://www.salesforce.com) can all do this.  Each have unique reasons for how those fields are they way they are such as the fact in the world there are over 42 billion doors and 100 million buildings, so the PBkey needs to handle key size of of true addresses or doors x buildings (42*10^18 combinations).

At my organization we figured out a work around using when and stringr fixed the issue neither if_else nor case_when fixed it.  The code was very messy.  However, I noticed that when "when" was depreciated, it did not go through the typical error checks.  These is why I am concerned about even a soft depreciation of when.

Both these two threads have brought up the causes listed here: https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/1004 and https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/1027

I am glad you found the cause for my concern especially with chain errors needing to bubble up.   However, I am still uncertain what version of 4.2 will come with the patch that fixes [https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=18346](https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=18346).  So until issue 1004 and 1027 are resolved, I would like to ask that when be un-depreciated.

title: incorrect concept of ellipsis in imap
description:
Sometimes I need to pass an ellipsis to the map-family functions. But there are problems.

Let's look at the problem with an example (JUST AN EXAMPLE):
```r
testFunc <- function(.object, ...) {
    purrr::imap(.object, ~{paste(c(.x, .y, 23), ...)}, ...)
}
testFunc(c('sd', 'cxd', 'wtf'), collapse = '+')
```

What i get:
```r
[[1]]
[1] "sd sd 1+1 sd 1+23 sd 1"

[[2]]
[1] "cxd cxd 2+2 cxd 2+23 cxd 2"

[[3]]
[1] "wtf wtf 3+3 wtf 3+23 wtf 3"
```

What i expect:
```r 
[[1]]
[1] "sd+1+23"

[[2]]
[1] "cxd+2+23"

[[3]]
[1] "wtf+3+23"
```

The reason is that the implementation of ellipsis in map does not allow me to do this.

```r
testFunc <- function(.object, ...) {
    purrr::imap(.object, ~{browser(); paste(c(.x, .y, 23), ...)}, ...)
}
testFunc(c('sd', 'cxd', 'wtf'), collapse = '+')

Called from: .f(.x[[i]], .y[[i]], ...)
Browse[1]> list(...)
[[1]]
[1] "sd"

[[2]]
[1] 1

$collapse
[1] "+"
```

As you can see, the ellipsis in the map function contains, in addition to the arguments I passed, also `.x` and `.y`.

Question: why?
1) It interferes with my idea
2) There is already one in the environment `.x` `.y`, why are their duplicates in `...`?

I have a request - please remove from `...` in map, the first 2 arguments are not needed, their presence is impractical.

P.S.: Workarounds of this jamb through do.call or something that requires passing a function not directly in the formula, but through "function" or something like that are categorically not suitable!

Acceptable crutch - if they explain to me how to remove from `...` the first 2 arguments. But in general, this is a bad decision.

The best solution is to remove the first 2 garbage arguments from `...` on the function side.

title: `purrr:::capture_output()` should use `conditionMessage()` not `$message`
`reduce_impl()` needs to name `error_call` something like `purrr_error_call`
description:
Like with `map_(..error_call)`, we need to rename the `error_call` arg of `reduce_impl()` to something less liable to conflict with user arguments passed through `...`

In tidyr, with dev purrr installed some snapshot tests change and I see this incorrect error call of `fn()`

``` r
library(tidyr)

df <- tibble(x = list(1:2), y = list(1:3))

# Used to say `unchop()` in the call
unchop(df, c(x, y))
#> Error in `fn()`:
#> ! In row 1, can't recycle input of size 2 to size 3.

#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. └─tidyr::unchop(df, c(x, y))
#>  2.   └─tidyr:::df_unchop(cols, ptype = ptype, keep_empty = keep_empty)
#>  3.     └─purrr::reduce(x_sizes, unchop_sizes2, error_call = error_call)
#>  4.       └─purrr:::reduce_impl(.x, .f, ..., .init = .init, .dir = .dir)
#>  5.         └─tidyr (local) fn(out, elt, ...)
#>  6.           └─cli::cli_abort(...)
#>  7.             └─rlang::abort(...)
```

This is due to `df_unchop()` calling `reduce()` and passing `error_call` through, but it gets captured early by `reduce_impl()` and isn't passed through to `unchop_sizes2()`.

I suggest that we rename all of these cases to `purrr_error_call` and `.purrr_error_call` (in cases when we dot the args, for consistency) to eliminate potential conflicts and have a consistent way to handle this

We should probably see if there are other places this can come up

title: `map_df()` doesn't preserve dimensions on deep-named tibbles
description:
Hi,

Sorry for the unclear title, I had a hard time formulating this.

When you create a tibble with named objects, you end up with a named list containing named vectors.

This is invisible to the user as `print()` is working on the outer names, but `map_df()` is working on the inner names.
This unexpectedly transposes data frames, as you can see in the following code. This is also the case in multi rows dataframes (try with `n=2`), and it can be easily missed.


``` r
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(0)
get_obj = function(n){
  c(w=round(rnorm(n)))
}

a = tibble(x=get_obj(1), y=get_obj(1))
dput(a)
#> structure(list(x = c(w = 1), y = c(w = 0)), class = c("tbl_df", 
#> "tbl", "data.frame"), row.names = c(NA, -1L))
a
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     0
a %>% map_df(~.x)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       w
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     1
#> 2     0
```

title: Concerns about if 1.0.0 really is user focused.
description:
After reading news in #999 and the reactions on the [twitter post](https://twitter.com/hadleywickham/status/1590457649396867072), I do not feel that the changes to core purpose of purrr aligns with how the packages is used by everyday non-developers.  These are the following reasons why..... 

**Major Concerns:**

"prepend(), rdunif(), rbernoulli(), when(), and list_along() have all been deprecated (#925). It's now clear that they don't align with the core purpose of purrr."

Why are rbernoulii and when being depreciated and not moved to separate package? In particular "when()" does not have a replacement prior to 4.2.2 because there are bugs in gsub that were only recently patched in the last few months.   Why don't simple make a wrapper to the proper function until the next major release of base R? We have strong concerns about the development of R packages and whether users have a voice or if everything has become developer focused.  It does not feel like the depreciation is gradual at all.   When myself and my teammates read the new changes, we truly felt that the developer of the packages either doesn't understand or they simple don't care how non-developers use there open source package. 

"*_dfc() and *_dfr() have been superseded in favor of using the appropriate map function along with list_rbind() or list_cbind() (#912)."

When I read this news I truly feel the developer of the packages don't understand how non-developers use there open source package. We have strong objections to this change and concern when combined with other changes it only allow users to purr over a limited number of R data frame types, classes, and most importantly environments.  

"lgl(), _int(), _int(), and _dbl() now use the same (strict) coercion methods as vctrs (#904). This means that..."  

So you are going to take vctrs, something that is arguably the worst implemented change in all of tidy verse history.  And now apply it to all of purr?   Your taking something that broke so much code and tutorials 3.6 and 4.0 that your now applying it to purr?  When I read this news I truely feel the developer of the packages don't understand how non-developers use there open source package.   How is this a gradual depreciation?  We have strong objections to this change and concern when combined with other changes it only allow users to purr over a limited number of R data frame types, classes, and most importantly environments.  

"map2(), modify2(), and pmap() now use tidyverse recycling rules where vectors of length 1 are recycled to any size but all others must have the same length (#878)." 

Is very confusing because it implies that first index, second index are the same length.  Why would use use map2 at all then?  Why have a second index or second anything if your first is the same?  How would anyone know how to use the package?  These index changes are an example of why the vctrs and dplyr principles don't make sense. It would make more sense to add a function to make recycling rules explicit. It would make even more sense not to touch the length of indexes at all.

title: Allow map_* to treat NULLs as NAs
description:
When working with sparse nested lists (like JSON), it is common to have missing keys or NULL values, which are difficult to coerce into a desired type with purrr.

For example:

``` r
list(list("a" = 1L), list("b" = 2L)) %>% map_int("a")
#> Error: Result 2 is not a length 1 atomic vector
```

We can achieve the desired effect by mapping twice and using the `null-replace` operator

``` r
> list(list("a" = 1L), list("b" = 2L)) %>% map("a") %>% map_int(`%||%`, NA)
#> [1]  1 NA
```

Ideally, `map_*` and `flatten_*` would treat `NULL`s as `NA`s, possibly by default or if not then by an argument. It could throw a warning when this occurs.

The options I see are:
1. Throw an error
2. Return a vector that excludes the `NULL` entries
3. Return a vector with appropriate `NA`s where `NULL`s were encountered

Currently, purrr implements option 1, which will lead to difficult to debug failures when working with JSON, and a lot of duplicated code to prevent it. I believe option 2 is very dangerous (this is what `unlist` does). Hence the suggestion for option 3.

title: Add warnings to `pluck()` and `chuck()` when accessors are factors
description:
I recently got very confused passing factor elements to `...` in `pluck(.x, ...)`. The factor is effectively unclassed into an integer vector, so elements of `.x` are accessed according to their position rather than their name.

This is all completely correct and consistent (as per reprex below), but it's probably very rarely what the user is expecting. I suspect that passing factors to `pluck()` or `chuck()` is almost always done in ignorance. 

Could we add warnings to these functions that tell the user they've probably done something they didn't mean to?

``` r
some_factor <- factor(c("foo", "bar", "baz"))
just_foo <- some_factor[1]

print(just_foo)
#> [1] foo
#> Levels: bar baz foo

a_list <- c(foo = "foo_value", bar = "bar_value", baz = "baz_value")

purrr::pluck(a_list, just_foo)
#> [1] "baz_value"

## It's consistent with base R, just confusing
a_list[[just_foo]]
#> [1] "baz_value"
a_list[["foo"]]
#> [1] "foo_value"

## Proposed "solution"
pluck_warn <- function(.x, ...){
  dots_list <- list(...)
  check_factors <- purrr::map_lgl(dots_list, is.factor)
  any_factors <- any(check_factors)
  
  if(any_factors) warning("Did you really mean to pass a factor to pluck?")
  
  purrr::pluck(.x, ...)
}

pluck_warn(a_list, just_foo)
#> Warning in pluck_warn(a_list, just_foo): Did you really mean to pass a factor to
#> pluck?
#> [1] "baz_value"
```

title: pmap with .f argument in function format generates strange errors.
description:
**Problem:**
1. In certain cases, running `purrr::pmap` with `.f` argument in function format generates strange error. 
2. There is no problem when using the formula format for `.f` argument.

When you have named list of lists for the `.l` argument and are using an anonymous function for the `.f` argument, you need to use the list names as arguments, e.g., if `.l = list(args_list_1 = ..., args_list_2 = ...)` then we must use `function(arg_list_1, arg_list_2) { ... }` rather than say `function(arg_1, arg_2) { ... }` which is what you could do in case you were utilising an un-named list of lists for .l argument . 

Kind of strange and unnecessary behaviour in my opinion. Comparing this R code with similar OCAML/F#: Pattern matching in R is definitely awkward or maybe ML languages somewhat spoil a person in such regards. 

**Solution 1:**
Use names of lists from within the `.l` lists of lists.

**Solution 2**
1. Use `base` lists rather than `tibble` lists to feed the `.l` argument.
2. Remove any naming beyond the actual arguments lists.

```verbatim
System     : Windows 10 x64                   (latest updates)
R Ver.     : "R version 4.0.2 (2020-06-22)"
Repo       : "https://mran.microsoft.com/"    (latest daily snapshot of CRAN)
purrr Ver. : "0.3.5"                          (latest tidyverse updates)
```

```r
library(purrr)

rnorm_args <- list(n = 2, mean = 0, sd  = 1)
runif_args <- list(n = 2, min  = 0, max = 1)
rand_arg   <- list(rnorm_args = rnorm_args, runif_args = runif_args)
rand_fn    <- list(rnorm_fn = rnorm, runif_fn = runif)
input      <- list(rand_fn = rand_fn, rand_arg = rand_arg)

# .f argument in formula format :  Works as expected
pmap(.l = input,
     .f = ~ exec(.fn = .x, !!!.y))
#> $rnorm_fn
#> [1] -3.4087219 -0.7465965
#> 
#> $runif_fn
#> [1] 0.8398340 0.2766491

# .f argument in function format: Generates Error
pmap(.l = input,
     .f = function(fn, args) exec(.fn = fn, !!!args))
#> Error in .f(rand_fn = .l[[1L]][[i]], rand_arg = .l[[2L]][[i]], ...): unused arguments (rand_fn = .l[[1]][[i]], rand_arg = .l[[2]][[i]])

# FIX 1: Use names of lists in input list
# .f argument in function format : NOW, It works as expected ..
pmap(.l = input,
     .f = function(rand_fn, rand_arg) exec(.fn = rand_fn, !!!rand_arg))
#> $rnorm_fn
#> [1]  0.4274880 -0.4521357
#> 
#> $runif_fn
#> [1] 0.3050558 0.8541712

# FIX 2: Remove names of lists: NOW, It works as expected ...
input <- list(rand_fn, rand_arg)
pmap(.l = input,
     .f = function(fn, args) exec(.fn = fn, !!!args))
#> $rnorm_fn
#> [1] 0.2278993 0.6803844
#> 
#> $runif_fn
#> [1] 0.4297577 0.5496519
```

title: Pass pronouns to anonymous functions
description:
Map and related functions expect a function as an argument. This function can be defined as either an anonymous function or a formula. The formula notation is nice because it lets you access pronouns (.x, .y, etc). However, in teaching R, I have also found it to be extraordinarily confusing for learners. In base R, `y ~ x` means something like "y is a function of/dependent on x" eg. (`plot(y ~ x)`, `lm(y ~ x, data=df)`). In `case_when()` it means the exact opposite (ie. `y~x` means "x is dependent on condition y). In `tribble()` its meaning seems entirely unrelated to either base R or `case_when()` and in map like functions it creates anonymous functions that seems sort of related to the base R use, but is kind of weird in being one-sided. Trying to explain all that to a learner (especially one without a programming/maths background) is difficult, to say the least.

Now that base R has a concise anonymous function syntax `\()` would it be possible to somehow allow this to use pronouns? Possibly via `...`. For example:

```r
mtcars |> 
  group_by("cyl") |> 
  group_modify(~ add_row(.x))
```
could be rewritten as
```r
mtcars |> 
  group_by("cyl") |> 
  group_modify(\(...) add_row(.x))
```
or
```r
mtcars$cyl |>
  map(~ .x*2)
```
could be rewritten as
```r
mtcars$cyl |>
  map(\(...) .x*2)
```

Why not just use named arguments in anonymous functions? Learners (everybody?) have a hard time coming up with good names, whereas consistent naming by using pronouns helps code readability. Secondly using `...` means that a learner can learn that the function to `group_modify()` (requires the grouped dataframe (`.x`), without having to know it also requires the grouping variable (`.y`).

title: Supersede lift functions instead of deprecating
Plan for `flatten()`, `simplify()` and friends
description:
I suggest we at least we mark `as_vector()`, `simplify()`, `simplify_all()`, `flatten()`, and `flatten_*()` as questioning and remove from the function index. The semantics of these functions are not super clear, and I'm not sure it's worth completely nailing them down because many of the problems they were originally designed to solve have moved into tidyr. Their use in their purrr docs reveals few compelling uses cases:

* `as_vector()` is only used in its own examples.

* `simplify()` (a version of `as_vector()` that returns `x` if it can simplify) isn't used at all. 

* `simplify_all()` is used with the output of `transpose()`. The most compelling use case is with `safely()` to get lists of error and results. But I suspect we could tackle this a different way, perhaps with a `list_transpose()` inspired by the work we've done in `unnest_longer()`/`unnest_wider()` or possibly powered by `vec_simplify()`.

* `flatten()` is only used in its own examples. I can see `flatten()` being useful in conjunction with `map()` but it might be easier to create the `flat_map()` functions directly.

Long term, if we do discover that `flatten()` and `simplify()` are useful enough to bother fully fleshing out their semantics, I'd suggest deprecating them and introducing new `list_flatten()` and `list_simplify()`.

Additionally, it might be worth deprecating `flatten_dfc()` and `flatten_dfr()` as they have poor semantics (#648, #757). They are similar to both `dplyr::bind_rows(x)` and `vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!x)`. If we think it's unappealing to recommend a vctrs function we could add `list_rbind <- function(x) vctrs::vec_rbind(!!!x)` (and similar for `list_cbind()`). I think we'd probably require individual elements to be data frames.

title: Bug: accumulate2 returns a list, not a vector
description:
The documentation for `accumulate` and `accumulate2` says that both functions return vectors ("A vector the same length of `.x` with the same names as `.x`"). In fact, `accumulate` returns a vector, but `accumulate2` returns a list.

## Expected behavior

`accumulate2` returns a vector

## Observed behavior

`accumulate2` returns a list

## Reprex

title: accumulate() issues with list output of one row
description:
This is an odd "bug" I've encountered. It is not unexpected given the functions used. So I'm both asking if there is a better way to do this or if the functionality should be updated. If this is beyond the scope of `purrr`, feel free to close.

I wish to accumulate a list of unique values into a cell, but when we accumulate on a single row, it returns a single value. This single value doesn't fit with the other outputs because they are lists. This

``` r
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

running_unique <- function(x, y) { unique(c(x, y)) }

# Example simple function use
running_unique(1, c(1, 12, 3))
#> [1]  1 12  3

# Example using accumulate
accumulate(1:3, running_unique)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] 1 2 3
accumulate(1, running_unique)
#> [1] 1


df <- tribble(
  ~a, ~b,
  1, 1,
  2, 1,
  2, 2
)
df
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>       a     b
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     2     1
#> 3     2     2

df %>%
  group_by(a) %>%
  mutate(accum = accumulate(b, running_unique))
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `accum`.
#> x Input `accum` must return compatible vectors across groups
#> i Input `accum` is `accumulate(b, running_unique)`.
#> i Result type for group 1 (a = 1): <double>.
#> i Result type for group 2 (a = 2): <list>.
```

<sup>Created on 2020-12-04 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

If we just focus on groups with more than one row, then all is well. Notice that even with one value, it works.

```
df %>%
  filter(a == 2) %>%
  group_by(a) %>%
  mutate(accum = accumulate(b, running_unique))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#> # Groups:   a [1]
#>       a     b accum    
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <list>   
#> 1     2     1 <dbl [1]>
#> 2     2     2 <dbl [2]>
```

title: Equivalent of has_element() for element names in a list?
description:
I'm wondering if there is a purrr function that detects whether an element with a given name appears in a list. For example, in the following code:
```
> library(purrr)
> ingredients <- list(tomatoes = 3, radishes = 5, cucumbers = 2)
```

I'm looking for a simple way to find out if the `ingredients` list contains "tomatoes".

I tried the `has_element()` function, but it only works with the values in a list, not the names:
```
> has_element(ingredients, "tomatoes")
[1] FALSE

> has_element(ingredients, 3)
[1] TRUE
```
This makes sense to me as you probably want to avoid the situation where you accidentally match a name in the list when you are looking to match a value instead.

I ended up writing a function like this:
```
has_element_named <- function(list, name){!is.null(list[[name]])}

> has_element_named(ingredients, "tomatoes")
[1] TRUE

> has_element_named(ingredients, "celery")
[1] FALSE
```
But this runs the same risk: that it will also match a value as well as the name:
```
> has_element_named(ingredients, 3)
[1] TRUE
```
This might be desirable in some circumstances, but most people will probably want to match against either names or values, not both. So I wrote:
```
has_element_called <- function(list, name){name %in% names(list)}

> has_element_called(ingredients, "tomatoes")
[1] TRUE
> has_element_called(ingredients, "celery")
[1] FALSE
> has_element_called(ingredients, 3)
[1] FALSE
```
Which is simple enough to do I guess, but there may be a better designed or robust function that  could be written (or maybe it already exists I just can't find it). This function doesn't, for example, account for any depth in the list you are matching against.

```
> a <- list(x = data.frame(one = 1, two = 2))
> b <- list(x = data.frame(three = 3))
> list_modify(a, b)
# current
$x
  one two three
1   1   2     3
# desired
$x

1     3
```

title: Option to preserve `accumulate()` length when `.init` is specified
description:
Is it possible to add an extra flag for inhibiting the length extension when `.init` is specified for `accumulate` function?

Rationale: there are situations when the `.init` is an important input value, but the result of the first accumulate step (having the value of the `.init`) is not required, just the subsequent values. 
This side effect of incrementing the length  makes it infeasible to use with tibbles.

For example, the subsetting works, but the legibility is questionable: 

```r
library(tidyverse)

numbers =  c(1, 2, 3)
numbers_df <- tibble(n = numbers)

numbers_df %>% 
  mutate(acc_init = accumulate(n, `+`, .init = 1000))
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` input `acc_init`.
#> x Input `acc_init` can't be recycled to size 3.
#> i Input `acc_init` is `accumulate(n, `+`, .init = 1000)`.
#> i Input `acc_init` must be size 3 or 1, not 4.

numbers_df %>% 
  mutate(acc_init = accumulate(n, `+`, .init = 1000)[-1])
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>       n acc_init
#>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1     1     1001
#> 2     2     1003
#> 3     3     1006

```
I think that a separate flag makes sense, because I assume that there are other cases when the extended length is preferred.

title: map_dfc() fails when the result contains list columns
description:
Sometimes we have a data.frame-like list and want to apply some function and harvest the result as data.frame. `map_dfc()` is quite useful for this purpose:

``` r
not_nested <- list(
  col1 = c("Apple", "Orange"),
  col2 = c("Baseball", "Football")
)

purrr::map_dfc(not_nested, purrr::map_chr, sprintf, fmt = "I like %s")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>            col1            col2
#>           <chr>           <chr>
#> 1  I like Apple I like Baseball
#> 2 I like Orange I like Football
```

But it fails if the result contains list columns:

```r
nested <- list(
  col1 = list(
    c("Apple", "Banana"),
    c("Orange")
  ),
  col2 = list(
    c("Baseball", "Soccer"),
    c("Football")
  )
)

purrr::map_dfc(nested, purrr::map, sprintf, fmt = "I like %s")
#> Error in cbind_all(x): Argument 2 must be length 2, not 1
```

Is it possible to get the result as data.frame like bellow?

``` r
tibble::as_tibble(
  purrr::map(nested, purrr::map, sprintf, fmt = "I like %s")
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>        col1      col2
#>      <list>    <list>
#> 1 <chr [2]> <chr [2]>
#> 2 <chr [1]> <chr [1]>
```

(As the error indicates, this seems up to `cbind_all()`. Should I file this issue to dplyr's repo?)

title: Should `pluck<-` actually be `chuck<-`?
description:
I am not sure that `pluck()` and `pluck<-()` are consistent. `pluck()` returns `NULL` if the element does not exist, but `pluck<-()` throws an error. In that way, `pluck<-()` feels more like the counterpart to `chuck()`. 

I am not sure that `pluck<-()` should even exist, since `assign_in()` is very strict and requires that the plucked-location must exist. I am just arguing that is should be named `chuck<-()` instead.

``` r
library(purrr)

pluck(mtcars, "y")
#> NULL

chuck(mtcars, "y")
#> Error: Can't find name `y` in vector

# should this be `chuck<-`()?
pluck(mtcars, "y") <- 1 
#> Error: Can't find name `y` in vector

# this should be `pluck<-`() I think
mtcars$y <- 1

# what I think should be `chuck<-`() uses chuck() already
`pluck<-`
#> function (.x, ..., value) 
#> {
#>     assign_in(.x, list2(...), value)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x7f9558ae34e8>
#> <environment: namespace:purrr>
purrr:::assign_in
#> function (x, where, value) 
#> {
#>     chuck(x, !!!where)
#>     call <- reduce_subset_call(quote(x), as.list(where))
#>     call <- call("<-", call, value)
#>     eval_bare(call)
#>     x
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x7f9558ae2790>
#> <environment: namespace:purrr>
```

title: `assign_in` and `modify_in` should create nested elements
description:
Current implementation of `assign_in`, `update_in` and `pluck<-` doesn't create new elements. 
This is in contrast to `[[<-` semantics and most importantly to the parallel functional tooling in other languages ([clojure](https://clojuredocs.org/clojure.core/assoc-in), [python](https://toolz.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api.html#toolz.dicttoolz.update_in)).


``` r
assign_in(list(), "aa", 34)
#> Error: Plucked object must have at least one element
pluck(list(), "aa") <- 34
#> Error in pluck(list(), "aa") <- 34: invalid (NULL) left side of assignment
```

Moreover, this is inconsistent with `pluck` itself which returns `NULL` on missing elements.  So one would expect no error for missing elements in `pluck<-` as well.

Seems related: #636

title: pass dots to anonymous function?
description:
I'm getting some weird behavior when trying to pass `...` arguments to anonymous functions, i.e., functions specified using `~`. I initially ran into this issue using `slider::slide2()` but I am reproducing the issue with `map2()` so I'm thinking the issue has to do with `as_mapper()`. The issue crops up when trying wrapping a function around `map()`, e.g. this reprex:

```r
library(purrr)

# a silly function
test_fun = function(x, mask, a = 5) {
  x[mask] = a
  x
}
# using map2_dbl
bar1 = function(x, mask, ...) {
  map2_dbl(x, mask, test_fun, ...)
}
# using map2_dbl and ~ function
bar2 = function(x, mask, ...) {
  map2_dbl(x, mask, ~ test_fun(.x, .y, ...))
}

set.seed(42)
xs = rnorm(10)
mk = as.logical(rbinom(10, 1, 0.5)) 

bar1(xs, mk, a = 3)
## [1]  3.0000000 -0.5646982  3.0000000  3.0000000  0.4042683  3.0000000
## [7]  1.5115220  3.0000000  2.0184237  3.0000000bar2(xs, mk)

bar2(xs, mk, a = 3)
## Error in test_fun(.x, .y, ...) : unused argument (TRUE)
```

In more complex cases I have gotten weird results where it appears that the components of `...` are getting mixed up or erroneously recycled from the initial two arguments. Is passing `...` to anonymous functions as in `bar2()` simply a no-go?

title: Deal with objects coercible to lists, such as GRangesList
description:
For some reason purrr::map() does not play well with CompressedGRangesList and GRangesList objects from GenomicRanges package. The base lapply has no such problems.

I suggest an improvement to be able to deal with these pseudo-lists. The class itself is coercible to a list with "as".

Example code:
```r
require(GenomicRanges)
require(purrr)
# init some variables:
gr1 <- GRanges(seqnames = "chr2", ranges = IRanges(3, 6), strand = "+", score = 5L, GC = 0.45)
gr2 <- GRanges(seqnames = c("chr1", "chr1"), ranges = IRanges(c(7,13), width = 3), strand = c("+", "-"), score = 3:4, GC = c(0.3, 0.5))
gr3 <- GRanges(seqnames = c("chr1", "chr2"),	ranges = IRanges(c(1, 4), c(3, 9)), strand = c("-", "-"), score = c(6L, 2L), GC = c(0.4, 0.1))
grl <- GRangesList("gr1" = gr1, "gr2" = gr2, "gr3" = gr3)


# this does not work:
grl %>% map(function(.) max(.$score))
Error: `.x` must be a vector, not a `CompressedGRangesList` object
Call `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace

# this works:
grl %>% lapply(function(.) max(.$score))
$gr1
[1] 5

$gr2
[1] 4

$gr3
[1] 6

# this works:
as(object = grl, Class = "list")

```

title: Use pmap to iterate rowwise without unpacking list columns?
description:
I have a tibble including list columns, and would have expected pmap to iterate over it row-wise like it would over any dataframe. Instead, it somewhat unnests the rows (retaining single-item lists), which increases the number of rows and makes it hard to reassemble results. Not sure whether that is a bug or a behavior that is just unexpected.

A minimum example where I would have expected the two calls to pmap to return the same output:

``` r
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
pmap(mtcars[1:3, ], ~tibble(...)$mpg)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 21
```

title: pluck(x, NULL) errs; use cases for why it shouldn't?
description:
This is tangentially-related to #480, but is manifested in a slightly different way, so I figured to open a new issue. Currently both of these throw errors:
```r
pluck(x, NULL)
pluck(x, character(0))
```
I think this might be too harsh. 

In #480, @jennybc mentions:

> It does seem sort of troubling that pluck() won't allow you to retain, say, character(0) vs NULL inside some workflow. Yet I don't have any current compelling example where this is harmful.

#### Workflow Example 1

One such use case (where `NULL` and/or `character(0)` are part of a workflow) is in Shiny apps. `shiny::radioButtons`, e.g., can be configured to have no default selection, in which case the reactive value server-side is `NULL`. If those radio buttons are used to pluck a dataset out of a list, the app author now needs to add additional code (admittedly, perhaps not **a lot** of additional code by using `shiny::req`) to check for the un-set case. Adding this additional code for some app improvement is great; needing to add additional code to prevent a `pluck` error feels less great, especially since `pluck` already has `.default` semantics. In the app case, for example, one might want to set `.default` to hard-coded example dataset for the rest of the app to use on initialization:
```r
output$some_output <- renderSomething({
  pluck(my_data, input$my_radio_buttons, .default = my_default_data_set) %>%
    downstream_processing()
})
```
^ That fails when `input$my_radio_buttons` is `NULL`. Adding additional `req` or `isTruthy` (or equivalent) logic simply to avoid the `pluck` error when `.default` is present seems cumbersome.

#### Workflow Example 2

Another workflow example is simply using `pluck` in one list to retrieve a value that is then used as a key when `pluck`-ing from another list:
```r
obj1 <- list(my_type = "type1", some = "other", data = "here")
obj2 <- list(
  foo = list(  ## just for the sake of inserting a nested list to demonstrate pluck's utility
    "type1" = c(some, stuff, here),
    "type2" = c(some, other, stuff, here)
  )
)
## let's retrieve my_type from obj1 and use that to fetch stuff from obj2:
pluck(obj2, "foo", pluck(obj1, "my_type"), .default = c(some, default, stuff))
```
^ That works great when "my_type" is present in `obj1`.
But if "my_type" is missing, the outer `pluck` throws an error because `pluck(obj1, "my_type")` resolves to `NULL`. So we have to add conditionals to short-circuit the outer `pluck` call, returning the `.default` in that case **and** keeping the `.default` in the outer `pluck` in the instances where "my_type" _is_ present in `obj1` but doesn't have a corresponding value in `obj2`.

In both such examples, there're clearly ways around this, mostly with lots of conditionals (or wrapping pluck in `tryCatch`), but the `.default` option in `pluck` feels like it was introduced to handle non-existent keys, and `NULL` feels like a non-existent key. Probably the same reasoning holds for `character(0)` (and other zero-length values passed as keys), but I can definitely see throwing errors when passed a length > 1 vector as a pluck element key. Likewise, `chuck()` should throw an error when given `NULL` as a key, as it's advertised as being strict.

title: Unexpected behavior of `lmap_if` when `.f` alters structure of `.x` and a function is supplied to  `.else`
description:
I was playing around with the `lmap_if` function and encountered an unexpected behaviour when a function is provided to `.else` while the function in `.f` is altering the structure of the object that `lmap_if` is applied to. This behavior might be intended, in this case please close this issue.

``` r
# setup
library(purrr)
```

Here is a simple function, similar to the one in the documentation. This function just duplicates
a list element.

``` r
list_rep <- function(x) {
  out <- rep_len(x, 2)
  names(out) <- paste0(names(x), 1:2)
  out
}
```

This is the example list from the documentation:
``` r
x <- list(a = 1:4, b = letters[5:7], c = 8:9, d = letters[10])
```

Lets apply `lmap_if` and say we want to duplicate each numeric list element and we want to
replace all other elements with `list(z = 1)`.

``` r
lmap_if(x, 
        .p = is.numeric,
        .f = list_rep,
        .else = ~ list(z = 1))
#> $a1
#> [1] 1 2 3 4
#> 
#> $z
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $b
#> [1] "e" "f" "g"
#> 
#> $z
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $c2
#> [1] 8 9
#> 
#> $d
#> [1] "j"
```

The output is somewhat unexpected. Rewritting `lmap_if` as a loop - at least the way I thought it would work - would yield the following result.

``` r
out <- vector("list", length = length(x))

for (i in seq_along(x)) {
  out[[i]] <- if (is.numeric(x[[i]])) {
    list_rep(x[i]) 
  } else {
    list(z = 1)
  }
}
out <- flatten(out)
out
#> $a1
#> [1] 1 2 3 4
#> 
#> $a2
#> [1] 1 2 3 4
#> 
#> $z
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $c1
#> [1] 8 9
#> 
#> $c2
#> [1] 8 9
#> 
#> $z
#> [1] 1
```

The reason for this unexpected behavior is that `lmap_if` creates an selector based on the function in `.p` and then applies `lmap_at` first on all selected elements (which might alter the structure of `.x`) and then applies `lmap_at` again at the result of the first operation using all elements which were not selected. However, since the selector was created before the first call to `lmap_at` it doesn’t necessarily match the structure of `.x` anymore. Is this behavior intended and was just my mental model of what `lmap_if` is doing wrong?

title: accumulate_n
description:
This parallels #253: it is useful to make a vector by applying a function recursively to an initial input for a set number of times. For example, you could use this to simulate a random walk or another type of martingale. 

Riffing on @dgrtwo's code, `accumulate_n()` would look something like this:
```
accumulate_n <- function(.x, .f, .n, ...) {
  .f <- as_function(.f, ...)

  ret <- vector("list", .n)
  ret[[1]] <- .x

  so_far <- .x

  for (i in seq(2, .n)) {
    result <- .f(so_far)
    ret[[i]] <- result
    so_far <- result
  }

  ret
}
````

This is easy to do in a for loop, but it is hard to pass that for loop to another function.  The idea came up today while working with @jkr216.

title: New comparison vignette
description:
Something like this:

---


One problem with the apply family is their lack of consistency:

-   The first argument to `lapply()`, `sapply()`, `vapply()` and `tapply()`, 
    is the vector; the first argument to `mapply()` is the function.

-   With `vapply()`, `sapply()`, and `mapply()` you can choose to
    suppress names on the output with `USE.NAMES = FALSE`; but you can't
    with `lapply()` or `tapply()`.

-   There's no consistent way to pass non-vectorised arguments on to the mapper
    function. Most functions use `...` but `mapply()` uses `MoreArgs` (which
    you'd expect to be called `MORE.ARGS` to be consistent with `USE.NAMES`). 
    The closely related  `Map()`, `Filter()` and `Reduce()` expect you to 
    create a new anonymous function.

-   `sapply()` and `mapply()` automatically simplify their output which
    means that different input lengths will return different _types_ of 
    output. `sapply()` has a variant that allows you to specify the desired 
    type called `vapply()`, but `mapply()` does not. Additionally, the 
    simplify argument to `sapply()` is called `simplify`; where for `mapply()`
    it's called `SIMPLIFY`.

Note that I don't mention `apply()` here; it has limited use because it works with matrices, which are rare in data analysis. You should never use `apply()` with a data frame because it turns it into a matrix, which is a slow operation.

title: map_dfr return a prototype when there are no iterations
description:
`map_dfr` returns a zero-column data frame if the input iterable has length zero. It would be nice to be able to provide a prototype as an argument, to guarantee some columns are always present in the output, even in corner cases where the input is empty.


```r
library(purrr)

y <- map_dfr(1, function(x) data.frame(x=1))
"x" %in% colnames(y) # This is TRUE
#> [1] TRUE

y <- map_dfr(integer(0L), function(x) data.frame(x=1))
"x" %in% colnames(y) # I would  like to provide a prototype to map_df so this becomes TRUE as well.
#> [1] FALSE
```

For instance

```r
y <- map_dfr(integer(0L), function(x) data.frame(x=1), .ptype = data.frame(x=numeric(0)))
"x" %in% colnames(y) # This would be TRUE
```

Would you think this feature would make sense?

Thanks for your time

title: flatten_df strips POSIXct class in top-level variables (related to #358 ?)
description:
When using `flatten_df` on a list, I expect the top-level variables in the output to have the same classes as before, yet this is not the case:

``` r
my_list <- list(a = lubridate::now(),
                b = list(f = 1, g = 2))

purrr::flatten_df(my_list)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>             a     f     g
#>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 1551127440.     1     2

# Expected output:
tibble::tibble(a = lubridate::now(), f = 1, g = 2)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   a                       f     g
#>   <dttm>              <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2019-02-25 21:44:00     1     2
```

(Tested in purrr `0.3.0` and also the current dev version from GitHub)
<sup>Created on 2019-02-25 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

I tried to find out if this is documented / intended behavior, but going by related issue #358, this is not intended, yet apparently fixed as the issue has been closed for a few months now and the thread indicates a successful PR.

Edit: Looking at the discussion of said PR, it looks like the implementation of `flatten_*` was not touched, so it makes sense that this issue is still present.

title: Extending map to handle higher-dimensional arrays
description:
It'd be handy if `map_*()` and `imap_*()` could handle functions returning higher-dimensional arrays, by gaining an output-shape parameter (defaulting to `1`). That is, if they were to behave like this generalization of `map_dbl()`:
```R
map_dbl <- function(.x, .f, ..., .shape = 1) {
  f <- as_mapper(.f)
  vapply(.x, f, FUN.VALUE = array(NA_real_, .shape), ...)
}
```
A typical use beyond the current capability of `map_*()` would be getting a matrix by mapping a function returning a vector (of a fixed length and type).

title: treat vctrs record rcrd as a list
description:
A vctrs record type, while implemented as a list (of equal-lengths vectors) under the hood, is otherwise treated as "atomic" externally (loosely speaking).
My naive expectation had been that `purrr::map()` would treat it thus and loop over it's length, not over the list of its internal structure.

``` r
library(vctrs)

new_rational <- function(n = integer(), d = integer()) {
  # assertions from vignette dropped
  new_rcrd(list(n = n, d = d), class = "vctrs_rational")
}

format.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) {
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")

  out <- paste0(n, "/", d)
  out[is.na(n) | is.na(d)] <- NA

  out
}

x <- new_rational(c(1, 1, 1), c(2, 2, 2))
# vctrs API sugggests a record, externally viewed, is NOT a list
vctrs::vec_is_list(x)
#> [1] FALSE
length(x)
#> [1] 3
# base R, oddly, agrees
lapply(x, str)
#>  vctrs_rt [1:1] 1/2
#>  vctrs_rt [1:1] 1/2
#>  vctrs_rt [1:1] 1/2
#> [[1]]
#> <vctrs_rational[1]>
#> [1] 1/2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> <vctrs_rational[1]>
#> [1] 1/2
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> <vctrs_rational[1]>
#> [1] 1/2
# but purrr treats a vctrs record as a list of *fields*
purrr::map(x, str)
#>  vctrs_rt [1:1] 1/2
#>  vctrs_rt [1:1] 1/2
#> $n
#> <vctrs_rational[1]>
#> [1] 1/2
#> 
#> $d
#> <vctrs_rational[1]>
#> [1] 1/2
```

<sup>Created on 2021-02-25 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

My expectation had been that `purrr::map()` would *not* break the external appearance of records and that, had I needed to get into the fields, I would have had to do that myself:

```r
map(x, function(i) {
  paste0(vctrs::field(i, "n"), vctrs::field(i, "d"))
})
```

---

Ps.: I've read many of the issues and lengthy discussions on `map()` and vctrs, and I hope this isn't a duplicate.
I'm guessing https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/495 is the closest one, though that's about implementing `vctrs::vec_map()`.

title: Feature: unfold function
description:
The functional programming language F# has a fantastic function that I believe should be considered for adding to purrr. It's basically the reverse of reduce/accumulate. It's the "[unfold](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualfsharpdocs/conceptual/seq.unfold%5B%27state,%27t%5D-function-%5Bfsharp%5D?f=255&MSPPError=-2147217396)" function and takes as an input:

1. an initial state
2. a function that takes a state and returns a state-option and a  value.

Unfold applies the function to the initial state, then if the result contains a new state the function is applied to that state, and this continues until the function stops returning a state.

As a practical example, if you wanted to make a sequence of all the powers of 2 under 1000, you could use unfold with:

1. initial state: `s <- 0`
2. a processing function: `f <- function(s) if((s+1)^2 < 1000) list(s+1, s^2) else list(NA, s^2)`

Then you would run `unfold(s, f)` to generate the sequence you want. You can also imagine that like reduce/accumulate you could have two versions, one that returns all the intermediate output and one that returns the final output only.

Here is a tweet by @ryantimpe where an unfold function would be perfect.   https://twitter.com/ryantimpe/status/1182705055549579264?s=20

Does this seem like something that could/should be added? If there is some interest I have a bunch more thoughts on how it could be implemented.

title: Could as_vector() and simplify() have some notion of .default?
description:
I want to promote elements of a list-column into a top-level variable, atomic if possible. But w/o having to say exactly which type I expect. `simplify()` comes really close, but there's no way to finesse NULLs.

Is there some better way to do this with current technology?

``` r
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

## imagine a tibble with a list-column that is homogeneous in the sense
## that, if an element is present, it has consistent type
(x <- tribble(
  ~ name, ~ stuff,
  "alpha", list(letter = "a", logical = TRUE),
  "beta", list(integer = 2L, logical = FALSE),
  "gamma", list(letter = "c", integer = 3L)
))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>    name      stuff
#>   <chr>     <list>
#> 1 alpha <list [2]>
#> 2  beta <list [2]>
#> 3 gamma <list [2]>

## to "promote" elements from the list-column into top-level vars
## I have to inject lots of info about type and NULL handling
x %>% 
  mutate(letter = map_chr(stuff, "letter", .default = NA_character_),
         integer = map_int(stuff, "integer", .default = NA_integer_),
         logical = map_lgl(stuff, "logical", .default = NA))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 5
#>    name      stuff letter integer logical
#>   <chr>     <list>  <chr>   <int>   <lgl>
#> 1 alpha <list [2]>      a      NA    TRUE
#> 2  beta <list [2]>   <NA>       2   FALSE
#> 3 gamma <list [2]>      c       3      NA
```

``` r
## I wish I could do this
x %>% 
  mutate(letter = simplify(map(stuff, "letter")),
         integer = simplify(map(stuff, "integer")),
         logical = simplify(map(stuff, "logical")))
```

``` r
## also tantalizingly close, but again the NULLs ruin everything
transpose(x$stuff, .names = c("letter", "integer", "logical")) %>%
  as_tibble()
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>      letter   integer   logical
#>      <list>    <list>    <list>
#> 1 <chr [1]>    <NULL> <lgl [1]>
#> 2    <NULL> <int [1]> <lgl [1]>
#> 3 <chr [1]> <int [1]>    <NULL>
```

title: flatten_names()
description:
To provide a way of combining names prior to flattening:

```r
x <- list(A = list(foo = 1, bar = 2), B = list(baz = 3)

  flatten_names(~paste(.x, .y, sep = " :: ")) %>%

#>
```

So this would work as well:

title: chuck() is a non-intuitive name
description:
It seems to me that `chuck()` should be the opposite of `pluck()`, rather than a strict form of `pluck()`.

Pluck means to take hold of (something) and quickly remove it from its place.
"she plucked a blade of grass"

Chuck means to throw (something) carelessly or casually.
"someone chucked a brick through the window"

So plucking something means you've selected something to keep.  Chucking something means you've chosen something to get rid of.  Yet if the element exists, `pluck()` and `chuck()` do the same thing.

As far as I can tell, there is actually no opposite to `pluck()`, where the list would be returned with everything except the element.

Suggestion:
1) Make clearer that `chuck()` doesn't actually discard/get rid of an element in the documentation.
2) Add a function that returns a list without the discarded element.  Perhaps `huck()`?

Huck means to throw (something).
"people have been hucking trash into the trees"

title: Support functions in `otherwise` parameter of `possibly()`
`compose` does not work for functions that modify experessions
description:
This seems to be best explained by an example (see reprex below). I am not sure whether this is expected behavior and `compose` is not intended for such purposes anyway, but for me, this was not obvious from reading its documentation. Considering that side-effects and metaprogramming are not uncommon and also not always obvious if you do not inspect the function body, this could be improved. 

If rewriting `compose` such that `compose(g, f)` and `function(...) g(f(...))` always evaluate to the same result is not feasible, suggest adding something to the `...` parameter documentation, e.g. *"Functions are expected not to perform meta-programming techniques on their arguments such as capturing and modifying expressions".* 

``` r
library(purrr)

fn1 <- compose(capture.output, print)
fn2 <- function(x) { 
  capture.output(print(x)) 
}

fn1("Hello, World!")
#> [1] "Hello, World!"
#> [1] "[1] \"Hello, World!\""
fn2("Hello, World!")
#> [1] "[1] \"Hello, World!\""
```

title: Format of printing in rate retry
description:
https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/blob/6ead03537e9c4395b55721421f87e41a3a5ec76b/R/rate.R#L317

I am using rate backoff for query retry logic and frequently get log messages like:

> Retrying in 6e+01 seconds.

My coworkers would like to see something like:

> Retrying in 60 seconds.

Is there a reason that I haven't thought of that using `sprintf` along with `%i` would not be preferred to the current implementation when values are coerced to integer?

title: Idea: having a `selectively()` adverb as an alternative to `*_if` functions.
description:
Many of the existing purrr functions already have `*_if` variants that allow users to apply a function to only those elements that satisfy a given predicate. But sometimes a user will want to use one of the functions that doesn't have an `*_if` variant with a predicate. An example might be if you wanted to make use of `modify_depth()`, but only modify the elements at a given depth that also satisfy a given predicate.

It would be possible to make variants that did this (eg. `modify_depth_if()`), but that seems unwieldy and confusing. One could also add `.p = ` arguments to all the functions, but that may also be confusing and couldn't be used beyond the purrr functions.

A more simple and elegant way to deal with this would be to have an adverb like `selectively()` which would take a function (`.f`) and predicate (probably `.p`) as inputs and return a new function that did the same thing as `.f` but only performed it on elements that satisfied `.p`. Elements that didn't satisfy `.p` would be left as is or optionally have an `.else` function applied to them as it is at the moment with the `*_if` functions.

In this form it would only work for applying a predicate test to the first argument of `.f`, but that already covers many use cases. I could imagine there being advanced variants that took more, perhaps like `selectively2()` for the first two arguments. There may also be a way to do it with named arguments or functions that take dots as their first argument.

A simple example would be something like this:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

times_ten <- function(x){x * 10}
is_more_than_two <- function(x){if(x > 2){TRUE}else{FALSE}}

number <- 1:5

tibble(number) %>% 
  mutate(ten_times_number = map_if(number, 
                                   is_more_than_two, 
                                   times_ten)) %>% 
  unnest(ten_times_number)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   number ten_times_number
#>    <int>            <dbl>
#> 1      1                1
#> 2      2                2
#> 3      3               30
#> 4      4               40
#> 5      5               50
```

<sup>Created on 2019-03-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

Instead you could write this to get the same output:

``` r
## doesn't work
tibble(number) %>% 
  mutate(ten_times_number = map_dbl(number, selectively(times_ten, 
                                                        .p = is_more_than_two))
```

<sup>Created on 2019-03-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

I like the idea of using `.if = ` rather than `.p = ` because it would read better, but for consistency with the other functions and to avoid confusion with the `if()` function it should probably be `.p =`.

Apologies if this has been mentioned elsewhere; I know there is the `when()` function, but the implementation of that looks different.

title: can insistently capture root cause error? (feature request)
description:
"insistently() and possibly() are a useful combination"  - from purrr documentation

The combination of safely + insistently I would argue could also be very useful IF insistently captured the root cause error not just that "the function failed after retrying X times"

Then we can have a system that gives a function multiple chances to succeed but if this doesn't happen we can control the output via safely's otherwise parameter  +  we keep a record of why the function failed. I would see this as a complete and effective way to work with APIs and R/tidyverse. Thanks.

title: modify_if() can't change a list element to NULL
description:
I can't find a way to set certain list elements to `NULL` with `modify_if()`. Any approach I've tried either removes the elements (which seems weird, because I thought `modify_*()` was size-stable) or creates an extra layer of list-nesting. This may be related to some other issues around pluck-y assignment and modify, such as #636, #634.

``` r
library(purrr)

(x <- list("a", "b"))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "b"

(x_I_want <- list("a", NULL))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> NULL

modify_if(x, ~.x == "b", NULL)
#> Error: Can't convert NULL to function
#> Backtrace:
#>     █
#>  1. ├─purrr::modify_if(x, ~.x == "b", NULL)
#>  2. └─purrr:::modify_if.default(x, ~.x == "b", NULL)
#>  3.   ├─purrr::as_mapper(.f, ...)
#>  4.   └─purrr:::as_mapper.default(.f, ...)
#>  5.     └─rlang::as_function(.f)
#>  6.       └─rlang:::abort_coercion(x, friendly_type("function"))

modify_if(x, ~.x == "b", ~ NULL)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a"

modify_if(x, ~.x == "b", ~ list(NULL))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a"
#>

#> NULL

modify_if(x, ~.x == "b", function(z) NULL)

modify_if(x, ~.x == "b", function(z) list(NULL))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]][[1]]
#> NULL
```

description:

``` r

 map(c("basic_information", "labels")) %>% 
 map(function(label) map_chr(label, ~ .x$name))
```

title: Function request: safely for walk varients
description:
I am trying to write a function to apply an arbitrary function (subject to a (data, ...) structure for its arguments, with data coercible to a data frame) to a set of files which are read from files, modified by the function, and then written back to files. This rather awkward construction is because many of these files are quite large -- collectively more than 40 GB -- so I can not hold all of them in memory at once. In addition, even fairly straightforward operations can be quite time consuming. So if my function bombs for some reason, I want a record of how and why and which one, but I do not want the whole sequence of files and computations to crash.

As I understand them, the current set of purrr analogs to try() -- safely(), possibly(), & quietly() -- all produce the complete output from the various purrr iteration functions as a single list object. This will I think often be inappropriate for long-running jobs that produce large objects or very large numbers of objects as output. It would be nice to have the informative "output, messages, warnings" structure of quietly() available for the walk family of functions that do not naturally reduce their output to a single object. Perhaps with an additional output for the iteration number or, for the case of a named input list, the iteration name, to assist in matching the errors with the relevant results.

title: a tidy equivalent to `ave()` ?
description:
`ave()` is the base functional I use the most if I attach *tidyverse*, but it has several issues : 

* Its name, and default, are awkward, I was a bit intimidated of this function as a beginner
* The doc is misleading, and only numeric input AND output are documented, so technically we "shouldn't" use it on characters and to return character for instance
* The `FUN` argument [must always be spelt explicitly](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26198908/why-this-simple-ave-function-is-not-working) as it comes after the dots
* We can't use *purrr* lambdas
* We can't pass additional arguments to dots, so many times we have to type a soul crushing (ok, maybe dramatizing a bit!) `FUN = function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`, when we'd really rather type `mean, na.rm = TRUE`
* `ave()` [can't output lists](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14551492/using-ave-with-function-which-returns-a-vector)
* Type stability (especially as `ave()` sometimes returns a ["wrong type"](https://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/ave-returns-wrong-type-td885247.html))
* It could play well with *vctrs*
* peformance could be improved it seems, given that [Hadley's remarks from 2010](https://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/Performance-enhancement-for-ave-td2271707.html) have not been considered as far as I can see

It might have been considered but since I found no relevant issues here it is.

Here's rough implementation (not type stable and not very efficient), to get my point across.

``` r
map_along <- function(.x, .along, .f, ...) {
  if (is.list(.along))
    .along <- interaction(.along) # as used by base::split.default
  .f <- rlang::as_function(.f)
  body <- as.call(c(quote(.f), quote(.x), eval(substitute(alist(...)))))
  fun <- rlang::new_function(alist(.x=), body)
  ave(.x, .along, FUN = fun)
}
map_along(c(1:4,NA),c(1,1,2,2,2), mean)
#> [1] 1.5 1.5  NA  NA  NA
map_along(c(1:4,NA),c(1,1,2,2,2), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 1.5 1.5 3.5 3.5 3.5
map_along(c(1:4,NA),c(1,1,2,2,2), ~mean(., na.rm = TRUE))
#> [1] 1.5 1.5 3.5 3.5 3.5
```

<sup>Created on 2020-01-13 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

A neat additional feature would be to have a magical function or pronoun to access the relevant instance of `.along` in the loop, `ave` doesn't support this and I missed it a few times (helps with debugging too).

title: aggregate identically named items
description:
When converting from xml for instance we might end up with a list featuring duplicate names, and it's a bit painful to deal with with current tools (unless I'm missing something).

R is not well equipped to deal with duplicate names, the *tidyverse* likes it even less, either imposing name repair or just failing (e.g. `dplyr::mutate_all()`), so I think it would make sense to have a function to preprocess this type of data.

At first I thought it might be an additional feature of `purrr::compact()`, as its also reducing the length by handling "anomalies", but I'm not sure if it goes well with its current `.p` feature (it might also be more of a *tidyr¨* thing ? I wasn't sure).

In my idea the function would take : 
* a list (incl. data frame)  
* a `combine()` aggregation function to apply on sets of identically named elements
* a `unname` boolean to optionally unname the dots fed to `combine()`.

I think having different defaults for data frame and bare list makes sense so by default on a list we'd just wrap the identically named elements in a list, and on a data.frame we'd repair the names and pack the columns.

Please find below sample data and a function draft : 

``` r
test_list <-
  list(0,
       a= 1, 
       a =2,
       b = c(3:4), 
       b = (5:6),
       c = list(7,8), 
       c = list(9,10),
       y = 11,
       z= NULL,
       12)

test_df <- tibble::as_tibble(test_list[-c(1,9,10)],.name_repair = "minimal")

compact2 <- function(
  x, 
  combine = if(is.data.frame(x)) tibble::tibble else list, 
  unname = rlang::is_bare_list(x)){
  combine <- rlang::as_function(combine)
  nms <- rlang::names2(x)
  # logical indices of named duplicates
  dupes_lgl <- duplicated(nms) & nms != ""
  # unique non empty names
  dupe_nms <- unique(nms[dupes_lgl])
  # replace first instance by combined value
  for(nm in dupe_nms){
    # subset of unnamed elements
    x_nm <- x[names(x) == nm]
    if(unname)
      x_nm <- unname(x_nm)
    else
      x_nm <- tibble::repair_names(x_nm)
    x[[nm]] <- do.call(combine, x_nm)
  }
  # ditch other instances
  x[dupes_lgl] <- NULL
  x
}
  
compact2(test_list)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $a
#> $a[[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $a[[2]]
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> 
#> $b
#> $b[[1]]
#> [1] 3 4
#> 
#> $b[[2]]
#> [1] 5 6
#> 
#> 
#> $c
#> $c[[1]]
#> $c[[1]][[1]]
#> [1] 7
#> 
#> $c[[1]][[2]]
#> [1] 8
#> 
#> 
#> $c[[2]]
#> $c[[2]][[1]]
#> [1] 9
#> 
#> $c[[2]][[2]]
#> [1] 10
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> $y
#> [1] 11
#> 
#> $z
#> NULL
#> 
#> [[7]]
#> [1] 12

compact2(test_list, c)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $a
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> $b
#> [1] 3 4 5 6
#> 
#> $c
#> $c[[1]]
#> [1] 7
#> 
#> $c[[2]]
#> [1] 8
#> 
#> $c[[3]]
#> [1] 9
#> 
#> $c[[4]]
#> [1] 10
#> 
#> 
#> $y
#> [1] 11
#> 
#> $z
#> NULL
#> 
#> [[7]]
#> [1] 12

compact2(test_list, ~sum(unlist(.)))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $a
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $b
#> [1] 7
#> 
#> $c
#> [1] 15
#> 
#> $y
#> [1] 11
#> 
#> $z
#> NULL
#> 
#> [[7]]
#> [1] 12

compact2(test_df)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>     a$a   $a1   b$b   $b1 c$c       $c1           y
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int> <list>    <list>    <dbl>
#> 1     1     2     3     5 <dbl [1]> <dbl [1]>    11
#> 2     1     2     4     6 <dbl [1]> <dbl [1]>    11
```

title: lift function to operate on list arguments in parallel
description:
I'd be interested in a `lift_` function that would convert functions to operate on parallel lists. 

Right now I use map if there's one argument or map2 if there are two, but would like an alternative with more flexibility for several named arguments.

One start is lifting `pmap` with `lift_ld`:

``` r
library(purrr)

lift_pmap <- function(.f) {
  lift_ld(pmap, .f = .f)
}
```

This works pretty well when every input is a vector or a list:

``` r
lift_pmap(sum)(1:2, 3:4)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 6
lift_pmap(sum)(1:2, list(3, 4))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 6

# works for individual vector inputs
lift_pmap(sum)(1:2, c(3, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2
```

There's an important variation where it fails, which is if certain arguments are not lists (or vectors of length 1/same length), but should be consistent for everything. For example:

``` r
mtcars_spl <- split(mtcars, mtcars$cyl)
fits <- lift_pmap(lm)(formula = mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars_spl)
#> Error: Element 1 is not a vector (language)
```

(Imagine there were multiple list arguments besides the formula). This is manageable with `pmap` but I find it a very counterintuitive order:

``` r
pmap(list(data = mtcars_spl), lm, formula = mpg ~ cyl)
```

Here is a start towards such a function that handles the above case. It suffers from the problem that argument order may be reshuffled and therefore need names. (That could be handled by instead converting non-list arguments to a list but there may be better ways; just leaving it here).

```
lift_pmap <- function(.f) {
  function(...) {
    lst <- list(...)

    is_vec_lst <- map_lgl(lst, ~ is.vector(.) || is.list(.))
    lst_args <- lst[is_vec_lst]
    same_args <- lst[!is_vec_lst]

    do.call(pmap, c(list(lst_args, .f), same_args))
  }
}

fits <- lift_pmap(lm)(formula = mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars_spl)
```

title: Having a function to replace the NULL
description:
I currently have a JSON that has this kind of structure : 

``` json
{
    "cars": {
        "Nissan": [
            {"model":"Sentra", "doors":4},
            {"model":"Maxima", "doors":4},
            {"model":"Skyline", "doors":2}
        ],
        "Ford": [
        ]
    }
}
```
When reading it, I've got a list with two sub elements, one being a df and the other an empty list : 

``` r
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")

write('{
    "cars": {
        "Nissan": [
            {"model":"Sentra", "doors":4},
            {"model":"Maxima", "doors":4},
            {"model":"Skyline", "doors":2}
        ],
        "Ford": [
        ]
    }
}', tmp)

cars <- jsonlite::fromJSON(tmp) 
cars
#> $cars
#> $cars$Nissan
#>     model doors
#> 1  Sentra     4
#> 2  Maxima     4
#> 3 Skyline     2
#> 
#> $cars$Ford
#> list()
```

If I map a nrow() on cars, I'll have a number and a NULL, which can't be reused as a vector or as a column for a tibble: 

``` r
library(purrr)
flat_cars <- cars %>%
  flatten() 

flat_cars
#> $Nissan
#>     model doors
#> 1  Sentra     4
#> 2  Maxima     4
#> 3 Skyline     2
#> 
#> $Ford
#> list()

tibble::tibble(
  model = names(flat_cars),
  n = map_int(flat_cars, nrow) 
)
#> Error: Result 2 must be a single integer, not NULL of length 0
#> Backtrace:
#> [removed]

# Or
tibble::tibble(
  model = names(flat_cars),
  n = map(flat_cars, nrow) 
)  %>% 
  tidyr::unnest()
#> Error: Each column must either be a list of vectors or a list of data frames [n]
#> Backtrace:
#> [removed]
```

My suggestion would be to have a function that changes the NULL to something. In the spirit of compact(), but instead allowing you to change NULL to something else (NA for example, which would be a nice default).

``` r
change_null <- function(.x, .with){
  modify(.x, function(x) if(is.null(x)) .with else x)
}

# In my case it makes sens to replace with 0 
tibble::tibble(
  model = names(flat_cars),
  n = map(flat_cars, nrow) %>% change_null(0)
) %>% 
  tidyr::unnest()
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   model      n
#>   <chr>  <int>
#> 1 Nissan     3
#> 2 Ford      0
```

title: Using `modify_at()` for removing elements
description:
Recently on Twitter there was a discussion about a tidy way of removing vector elements given their names ([this tweet](https://twitter.com/skyetetra/status/1187221129162711040) in particular).
I suggested `modify_at(x, names_to_remove, ~NULL)`, but it failed to work with multiple elements (thanks to [this tweet](https://twitter.com/EFromTheWest/status/1188126879787687937) from EFromTheWest user):
``` r
x <- list(a = 10, b = 15, c = 18, d = 9)
names_to_drop <- c("a", "b", "c")
purrr::modify_at(x, names_to_drop, ~NULL)
#> $b
#> [1] 15
#> 
#> $d
#> [1] 9
```

<sup>Created on 2019-10-26 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

This seems to be because internally `modify_at()` uses `modify_if()`, which in turn is implemented with iterative modification based on integer indexes (see [these lines](https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/blob/a8ec9032058e81c20f688523cbf129e0aaf22efd/R/modify.R#L154-L160)). This approach fails to work if elements are removed as a result of modification.

This issue is created to notify about this possible confusion and, probably, for you to consider supporting this behavior.

title: Data masking inside pmap() when value for data mask is provided by a column

title: compose should propagate all arguments to all functions
description:
Currently composed function passes its arguments to the first function only. This is not very useful, nor particularly meaningful. There is no reason why first function should be special in this regard. 

IMO the signature of compose should be ... and it should propagate all arguments to each function. 

A more involved implementation could filter arguments passed to composed function to match the signature of each function but this might be an overkill.

``` r
library(purrr)
tt <- compose(function(x, a = 1, ...) list_modify(x, a = a),
              function(x, b = 1, ...) list_modify(x, b = b),
              .dir = "forward")
tt(list(), a = 2, b = 2)
#> $a
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $b
#> [1] 1
```

title: Behavior of `*_at()` functions with unnamed input
description:
After using `*_at()` functions, I feel like their behavior is a little inconsistent. In documentation it says "`modify_at()` only modifies elements given by names or positions." and "Only those elements corresponding to `.at` will be modified." I read this as: try finding elements specified in `.at` and modify them, while not touching anything else.

When `.at` is a string, it works exactly like that when at least one list element is named. However, it throws error when there are no names, in which case I'd expect it to not find any `.at` elements and modify nothing while returning the input.

A reprex:
``` r
library(purrr)

map_at(list(1, a = 2), .at = "a", ~. + 1)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $a
#> [1] 3
map_at(list(1, b = 2), .at = "a", ~. + 1)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $b
#> [1] 2

map_at(list(1, 2), .at = "a", ~. + 1)
#> Error: character indexing requires a named object
modify_at(list(1, 2), .at = "a", ~. + 1)
#> Error: character indexing requires a named object
```
